# Atwell Mill Grove
United States
Atwell Mill Grove. Photo via Wikimedia Commons.
Atwell Mill Grove is a giant sequoia grove in the east fork of the Kaweah watershed area in California. Can be accessed via the Mineral King Road which branches off California State Route 198 below the south entrance to Sequoia National Park. The grove is located about 1.5 miles (2.4 km) west of the community of Silver City and 19 miles (31 km) from the junction of highway 198. The road into this section of the park is narrow and difficult. Atwell Mill Campground, on East Fork of the Kaweah River, is located in part of the grove that was logged before the trees were protected. Atwell Mill was at one time a lumber mill that processed logs from the grove.

# Atwell Mill Grove
United States
Atwell Mill Grove. Photo via Wikimedia Commons.
Atwell Mill Grove is a giant sequoia grove in the east fork of the Kaweah watershed area in California. Can be accessed via the Mineral King Road which branches off California State Route 198 below the south entrance to Sequoia National Park. The grove is located about 1.5 miles (2.4 km) west of the community of Silver City and 19 miles (31 km) from the junction of highway 198. The road into this section of the park is narrow and difficult. Atwell Mill Campground, on East Fork of the Kaweah River, is located in part of the grove that was logged before the trees were protected. Atwell Mill was at one time a lumber mill that processed logs from the grove.

**John Sutter** (born February 15, 1803, Kandern, Baden [Germany]—died June 18, 1880, Washington, D.C.) was a German-born Swiss pioneer settler and colonizer in California. The discovery of gold on his land in 1848 precipitated the California Gold Rush.
Sutter's MillSutter's Mill on the American River, Coloma, California; engraving, _Illustrated History of Plumas, Lassen & Sierra Counties, with California from 1513 to 1850_, 1882.(more)
Sutter spent much of his early life in Switzerland; he was a Swiss citizen and served in the Swiss army. Fleeing from bankruptcy and financial failures and leaving his wife and children in Switzerland, he reached California in 1839 and persuaded the Mexican governor to grant him lands on the Sacramento River. There, at its junction with the American River, he established the colony of Nueva Helvetia (New Switzerland), later to become Sacramento. He built “Sutter’s Fort” (1841), set up frontier industries, and, in spite of his enormous debts, provided lavish hospitality, and often employment, to traders, trappers, and immigrants who came to his fort. Sutter was much less accommodating to the local Native Americans whose labour he exploited.
James W. Marshall testing a gold nuggetJames W. Marshall and Mrs. Wimmer testing one of the first gold nuggets found at Sutter's Mill by boiling it in lye soap; illustration, _California Gold Book: First Nugget, Its Discovery and Discoverers_, by William Wallace Allen and R.B. Avery, 1893.(more)

# John Sutter
Discovery of gold on his land brought disaster to Sutter. In the process of building a water-powered sawmill, a carpenter named James W. Marshall found flakes of gold in a streambed (January 24, 1848). The two men tried to keep the find a secret, but the news leaked out. Workers deserted the colony. Gold seekers and squatters overran Sutter’s land, stealing and destroying his goods and livestock. When the U.S. courts denied title to his Mexican grants, his ruin was complete. By 1852 he was bankrupt.
Sutter's Mill replica Replica of Sutter's Mill, Marshall Gold Discovery State Historic Park, Coloma, California.(more)
In the early 1850s Sutter moved to Hock Farm, his estate on the Feather River, and in 1864 he was awarded a monthly pension by the California legislature. The following year, however, arsonists destroyed his home, and by 1871 Sutter had settled in Lititz, Pennsylvania. He frequently traveled to Washington, D.C., continuing his attempt to gain redress through the U.S. Congress. Sutter Street, in San Francisco, and Sutter County commemorate his name.
The Sutter story was retold in the 1985 song _Sutter’s Mill_ by American singer and songwriter Dan Fogelberg.

*   What was the California Gold Rush?
The California Gold Rush was a period of rapid migration to California following the discovery of gold at Sutter's Mill in early 1848. This event triggered an influx of over 300,000 fortune seekers, known as "forty-niners," by 1852.
The arduous journeys involved sailing around Cape Horn, crossing the Isthmus of Panama, or undertaking a 2,000-mile overland route, with disease often proving more deadly than conflict. While an estimated $2 billion in gold was extracted, few prospectors became wealthy due to hard labor, high prices, and primitive living conditions. The Gold Rush significantly altered California's demographics, hastening its statehood in 1850 and leading to the growth of cities like San Francisco.

# California Gold Rush
John Augustus SutterThe discovery of gold on Sutter's land in 1848 started the California Gold Rush. (more)
In 1848 John Sutter was having a water-powered sawmill built along the American River in Coloma, California, approximately 50 miles (80 km) east of present-day Sacramento. On January 24 his carpenter, James W. Marshall, found flakes of gold in a streambed. Sutter and Marshall agreed to become partners and tried to keep their find a secret. News of the discovery, however, soon spread, and they were besieged by thousands of fortune seekers. (With his property overrun and his goods and livestock stolen or destroyed, Sutter was bankrupt by 1852.) From the East, prospectors sailed around Cape Horn or risked disease hiking across the Isthmus of Panama. The hardiest took the 2,000-mile (3,220-km) overland route, on which cholera proved a far greater killer than the Native Americans. By August 1848, 4,000 gold miners were in the area, and within a year about 80,000 “forty-niners” (as the fortune seekers of 1849 were called) had arrived at the California goldfields. By 1853 their numbers had grown to 250,000. Although it was estimated that some $2 billion in gold was extracted, few of the prospectors struck it rich. The work was hard, prices were high, and living conditions were primitive.

# California Gold Rush
In what was a typical pattern, the Gold Rush slackened as the most-workable deposits were exhausted and organized capital and machinery replaced the efforts of individual miner-adventurers with more efficient and businesslike operations. Likewise, the lawless and violent mining camps gave way to permanent settlements with organized government and law enforcement. Those settlements that lacked other viable economic activities soon became ghost towns after the gold was exhausted. The California Gold Rush peaked in 1852, and by the end of the decade, it was over.

The Gold Rush had a profound impact on California, dramatically changing its demographics. Before the discovery of gold, the territory’s population was approximately 160,000, the vast majority of whom were Native Americans. By about 1855, more than 300,000 people had arrived. Most were Americans, though a number of settlers also came from China, Europe, and South America. The massive influx gave rise to numerous cities and towns, with San Francisco gaining particular prominence. The Gold Rush was credited with hastening statehood for California in 1850.

_\_\\_\\\_\\\\_How a shrewd Gold Rush businesswoman built a fortune, backed the abolitionist cause, and took racial exclusion in San Francisco to court — while carefully controlling the story of her own life.\\\\_\\\_\\_\__
By the time Mary Ellen Pleasant died in San Francisco in 1904, she had been called a millionaire, a capitalist, a voodoo queen, a madam, and the mother of California’s civil rights movement — sometimes all in the same newspaper column.1
She was one of the most influential Black women in Gold Rush–era San Francisco. Using inherited capital, business skill, and carefully cultivated networks, Pleasant built wealth through lending, gold-and-silver exchange, real estate, mining stock, boardinghouses, and other ventures. She supported abolitionist and Black civic causes, and later challenged racial exclusion on San Francisco streetcars through the courts.1
She was also one of the hardest historical figures to pin down. Pleasant gave differing accounts of her own beginnings, while newspapers and later biographers added layers of rumor and legend. More than a century after her death, historians are still working to separate the documented woman from the mythology surrounding her.2
Mary Ellen Pleasant, San Francisco pioneer, 1901. Miriam Matthews Photograph Collection, UCLA Library Digital Collections.9

## A Story With Many Beginnings
Even the basic facts of Mary Ellen Pleasant’s early life remain disputed. Pleasant said that she was born free in Philadelphia in 1819, while later accounts — including the semi-fictionalized biography _Mammy Pleasant_ — claimed she had been born enslaved in Georgia. The surviving record does not settle the question; what is clear is that, by the 1820s, she was living in Nantucket, Massachusetts.2
In Nantucket, Pleasant worked as a shop clerk and later described the experience as the beginning of her business education. She recalled learning to manage transactions and customers quickly in the busy store environment.2

## A Story With Many Beginnings
### Nantucket and the Hussey Store
The shop belonged to a family remembered as the Husseys. Pleasant became close with the family’s granddaughter, Phebe Hussey Gardner, and stayed in touch with her Nantucket connections for decades, even after she left the island around 1840 and began working more directly within the abolitionist movement.3

## A Story With Many Beginnings
### Boston, Abolition, and Two Marriages
Pleasant later moved to Boston, where she met James Smith, an abolitionist of some means. When Smith died in the 1840s, he left her capital that helped finance her move west. Pleasant later married John James Pleasant, and accounts place her arrival in San Francisco during the early 1850s, though the precise date remains disputed.2

## A Story With Many Beginnings
### Gold Fever and a New Life in San Francisco
John James Pleasant sailed for San Francisco not long after news of the 1848 gold discovery reached the East Coast, finding work as a ship’s cook. Sources differ on whether Pleasant arrived in 1849 or 1852; most accounts place her in San Francisco during the early Gold Rush boom, when the city’s rapid expansion created opportunities in lodging, domestic service, finance, and real estate.2

## From Housekeeper to Capitalist
_San Francisco’s harbor in 1851, photographed during the Gold Rush boom. Sterling C. McIntyre, Library of Congress.8_
Pleasant arrived with inherited capital and put it to work through lending, investment, and business ventures.1
At the same time, she worked as a housekeeper for some of San Francisco’s prominent merchants.1
Over time, her investments expanded dramatically. She became a major investor in real estate and mining stock, with property that eventually extended across the bay to Oakland, and built a financial position unusual for any woman in mid-nineteenth-century San Francisco. She was notoriously guarded about the exact scope of her fortune, a caution that historians attribute partly to savvy and partly to the very real legal and social risks a Black woman of enormous wealth faced in nineteenth-century California.2

## The “Black City Hall”
Pleasant used her wealth and connections in support of San Francisco’s Black community.1 Black newcomers could turn to her network for employment, housing, and practical assistance, and she became so well known as a community resource that she acquired one of her most memorable nicknames: the “Black City Hall.”7
She also contributed to the Athenaeum Building, a library and gathering place for San Francisco’s Black residents, and supported the Black press and the African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church.1

## Financing Freedom: Pleasant and John Brown
Near the end of her life, Pleasant told a reporter that she had helped finance John Brown’s 1859 raid on the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry.1
Pleasant said she had traveled to Canada, met with Brown, and supplied money for his plans. She also claimed authorship of a note associated with Brown and said that her initials had been misread, helping conceal her identity after the raid failed.7
In Pleasant’s telling, she then abandoned her original return ticket and traveled back toward California under less conspicuous circumstances.7
The account became one of the most famous episodes in Pleasant’s biography. But it comes principally from recollections she gave late in life, and documentary support for all of its details is limited. What is much more firmly established is Pleasant’s longstanding involvement in abolitionist circles and her admiration for Brown.2
By her own account, she kept this claimed role a closely held secret for the rest of her life, sharing it only in her final years. She requested that her tombstone identify her simply as “a friend of John Brown” — an inscription not actually added to her grave marker until 1965, more than sixty years after her death.1

## Mother of California’s Civil Rights Movement
Pleasant’s activism did not end with the Civil War. San Francisco’s horse-drawn streetcars in the 1860s frequently excluded Black passengers, and Pleasant became one of the people who challenged that practice.4

## Mother of California’s Civil Rights Movement
### The Streetcar Cases
In 1866, she brought a complaint after being denied service by one streetcar company. Contemporary accounts indicate that she withdrew that complaint after company officials agreed that Black passengers would be permitted to ride.7
Her second case produced a longer legal fight.
Pleasant attempted to board a car operated by the North Beach and Mission Railroad Company while her friend Elizabeth “Lisette” Woodworth was already aboard. Evidence introduced in the resulting case attributed a blunt response to the conductor:
_“We don’t take colored people in the cars.”_ 5
Pleasant sued.
A jury initially awarded Pleasant $500 in damages. The railroad appealed, and in 1868 the California Supreme Court reversed that award, finding insufficient proof of a willful injury by the company.5
The litigation nonetheless mattered. Pleasant’s case became part of a broader series of legal and civic challenges to racial exclusion on San Francisco transit. Later institutional summaries describe the case as helping to end segregated public transportation in the city, but that broader characterization should be distinguished from the appellate court’s narrower reversal of her damages judgment.6

## Mother of California’s Civil Rights Movement
### A Change in the Law
Pleasant has also been associated with the successful campaign to repeal California’s restriction on Black testimony against white defendants. The law was repealed in 1863, although the precise extent of Pleasant’s personal role is less firmly documented than her later streetcar litigation.4
Between her legal efforts, her financial support for civil rights causes, and her decades of direct assistance to formerly enslaved people building new lives in California, Pleasant became known by a title still used to describe her today: the mother of civil rights in California.4

## Wealth, Scandal, and “Mammy Pleasant”
Historians describe Pleasant as someone who carefully controlled public information about her finances, alliances, and past — a plausible form of self-protection for a wealthy Black woman operating in nineteenth-century San Francisco.2
Pleasant’s later years were shadowed by a business partnership and a controversy that would follow her reputation long after her death. In the 1870s, following her husband’s death, she began investing alongside a wealthy banker, Thomas Bell, and the two built an extensive, closely intertwined financial partnership that included a shared mansion at Bush and Octavia Streets.7
In 1892, the pair purchased a ranch in Sonoma Valley, and their finances remained deeply entangled even after Bell married a much younger woman named Teresa.7 After Bell died from a fall in 1892, his family and Pleasant became locked in lengthy litigation over their deeply intertwined finances. Pleasant ultimately lost control of much of the wealth and property associated with the partnership.7
The legal battles were accompanied by sensational newspaper coverage. Reporters increasingly called her “Mammy Pleasant,” a name Pleasant herself objected to.7
Newspapers also repeated accusations involving fraud, manipulation, and the occult. Those stories became part of the mythology that accumulated around Pleasant and have made it particularly difficult for historians to reconstruct her later life with confidence.2
The Bell/Pleasant residence at Bush and Octavia became central to Pleasant’s later business and legal conflicts. The building no longer stands.10
Pleasant was ultimately declared insolvent before her death in 1904, making the reversal from her earlier financial success all the more striking. Whatever the exact size of her fortune at its height — and estimates vary widely — she had spent decades as a significant investor and property owner in San Francisco.2
According to a later account, Pleasant spent her final months working with a Nevada journalist to record her own version of her life — an attempt to preserve her own account of a life increasingly surrounded by competing stories.7

## Legacy and Civic Relevance
Mary Ellen Pleasant’s life resists a simple summary, and that may be part of why she remains such a compelling figure in California history.
She arrived in Gold Rush San Francisco with capital and multiplied it through investment, property, and business. She used money and influence in support of abolitionist causes and San Francisco’s Black community. She challenged racial exclusion on public transportation through the courts. And by the end of her life, she had become surrounded by enough conflicting stories, lawsuits, newspaper accusations, and self-created mystery that historians are still working to establish where documentation ends and legend begins.2
Her story offers several unusually rich civic questions.
How can an individual use courts to challenge the conduct of powerful institutions? What roles do property, entrepreneurship, philanthropy, churches, newspapers, and civic networks play in building influence outside government? And how should historians evaluate a public figure when autobiographical accounts, court records, newspapers, and later recollections do not always agree?
Pleasant’s life brings all of those questions together. She was simultaneously a businesswoman, investor, abolitionist, litigant, philanthropist, and one of nineteenth-century San Francisco’s most elusive public figures.
Whatever uncertainty remains about Mary Ellen Pleasant’s birthplace, the exact size of her fortune, or some of the stories she told about her own life, the documented record is remarkable enough: she became a successful capitalist in Gold Rush San Francisco, supported abolitionist and Black civic causes, built an extensive network of businesses and property, and challenged racial exclusion through the courts.
Her life accumulated titles, accusations, fortunes, lawsuits, and legends.
But when Pleasant considered how she wanted to be remembered, she chose something much simpler:
**_A friend of John Brown._**

_\_\\_\\\_\\\\_How a shrewd Gold Rush businesswoman built a fortune, backed the abolitionist cause, and took racial exclusion in San Francisco to court — while carefully controlling the story of her own life.\\\\_\\\_\\_\__
By the time Mary Ellen Pleasant died in San Francisco in 1904, she had been called a millionaire, a capitalist, a voodoo queen, a madam, and the mother of California’s civil rights movement — sometimes all in the same newspaper column.1
She was one of the most influential Black women in Gold Rush–era San Francisco. Using inherited capital, business skill, and carefully cultivated networks, Pleasant built wealth through lending, gold-and-silver exchange, real estate, mining stock, boardinghouses, and other ventures. She supported abolitionist and Black civic causes, and later challenged racial exclusion on San Francisco streetcars through the courts.1
She was also one of the hardest historical figures to pin down. Pleasant gave differing accounts of her own beginnings, while newspapers and later biographers added layers of rumor and legend. More than a century after her death, historians are still working to separate the documented woman from the mythology surrounding her.2
Mary Ellen Pleasant, San Francisco pioneer, 1901. Miriam Matthews Photograph Collection, UCLA Library Digital Collections.9
texts.1:
## A Story With Many Beginnings
Even the basic facts of Mary Ellen Pleasant’s early life remain disputed. Pleasant said that she was born free in Philadelphia in 1819, while later accounts — including the semi-fictionalized biography _Mammy Pleasant_ — claimed she had been born enslaved in Georgia. The surviving record does not settle the question; what is clear is that, by the 1820s, she was living in Nantucket, Massachusetts.2
In Nantucket, Pleasant worked as a shop clerk and later described the experience as the beginning of her business education. She recalled learning to manage transactions and customers quickly in the busy store environment.2
texts.2:
## A Story With Many Beginnings
### Nantucket and the Hussey Store
The shop belonged to a family remembered as the Husseys. Pleasant became close with the family’s granddaughter, Phebe Hussey Gardner, and stayed in touch with her Nantucket connections for decades, even after she left the island around 1840 and began working more directly within the abolitionist movement.3
texts.3:
## A Story With Many Beginnings
### Boston, Abolition, and Two Marriages
Pleasant later moved to Boston, where she met James Smith, an abolitionist of some means. When Smith died in the 1840s, he left her capital that helped finance her move west. Pleasant later married John James Pleasant, and accounts place her arrival in San Francisco during the early 1850s, though the precise date remains disputed.2
texts.4:
## A Story With Many Beginnings
### Gold Fever and a New Life in San Francisco
John James Pleasant sailed for San Francisco not long after news of the 1848 gold discovery reached the East Coast, finding work as a ship’s cook. Sources differ on whether Pleasant arrived in 1849 or 1852; most accounts place her in San Francisco during the early Gold Rush boom, when the city’s rapid expansion created opportunities in lodging, domestic service, finance, and real estate.2
texts.5:
## From Housekeeper to Capitalist
_San Francisco’s harbor in 1851, photographed during the Gold Rush boom. Sterling C. McIntyre, Library of Congress.8_
Pleasant arrived with inherited capital and put it to work through lending, investment, and business ventures.1
At the same time, she worked as a housekeeper for some of San Francisco’s prominent merchants.1
Over time, her investments expanded dramatically. She became a major investor in real estate and mining stock, with property that eventually extended across the bay to Oakland, and built a financial position unusual for any woman in mid-nineteenth-century San Francisco. She was notoriously guarded about the exact scope of her fortune, a caution that historians attribute partly to savvy and partly to the very real legal and social risks a Black woman of enormous wealth faced in nineteenth-century California.2
texts.6:
## The “Black City Hall”
Pleasant used her wealth and connections in support of San Francisco’s Black community.1 Black newcomers could turn to her network for employment, housing, and practical assistance, and she became so well known as a community resource that she acquired one of her most memorable nicknames: the “Black City Hall.”7
She also contributed to the Athenaeum Building, a library and gathering place for San Francisco’s Black residents, and supported the Black press and the African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church.1
texts.7:
## Financing Freedom: Pleasant and John Brown
Near the end of her life, Pleasant told a reporter that she had helped finance John Brown’s 1859 raid on the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry.1
Pleasant said she had traveled to Canada, met with Brown, and supplied money for his plans. She also claimed authorship of a note associated with Brown and said that her initials had been misread, helping conceal her identity after the raid failed.7
In Pleasant’s telling, she then abandoned her original return ticket and traveled back toward California under less conspicuous circumstances.7
The account became one of the most famous episodes in Pleasant’s biography. But it comes principally from recollections she gave late in life, and documentary support for all of its details is limited. What is much more firmly established is Pleasant’s longstanding involvement in abolitionist circles and her admiration for Brown.2
By her own account, she kept this claimed role a closely held secret for the rest of her life, sharing it only in her final years. She requested that her tombstone identify her simply as “a friend of John Brown” — an inscription not actually added to her grave marker until 1965, more than sixty years after her death.1
texts.8:
## Mother of California’s Civil Rights Movement
Pleasant’s activism did not end with the Civil War. San Francisco’s horse-drawn streetcars in the 1860s frequently excluded Black passengers, and Pleasant became one of the people who challenged that practice.4
texts.9:
## Mother of California’s Civil Rights Movement
### The Streetcar Cases
In 1866, she brought a complaint after being denied service by one streetcar company. Contemporary accounts indicate that she withdrew that complaint after company officials agreed that Black passengers would be permitted to ride.7
Her second case produced a longer legal fight.
Pleasant attempted to board a car operated by the North Beach and Mission Railroad Company while her friend Elizabeth “Lisette” Woodworth was already aboard. Evidence introduced in the resulting case attributed a blunt response to the conductor:
_“We don’t take colored people in the cars.”_ 5
Pleasant sued.
A jury initially awarded Pleasant $500 in damages. The railroad appealed, and in 1868 the California Supreme Court reversed that award, finding insufficient proof of a willful injury by the company.5
The litigation nonetheless mattered. Pleasant’s case became part of a broader series of legal and civic challenges to racial exclusion on San Francisco transit. Later institutional summaries describe the case as helping to end segregated public transportation in the city, but that broader characterization should be distinguished from the appellate court’s narrower reversal of her damages judgment.6
texts.10:
## Mother of California’s Civil Rights Movement
### A Change in the Law
Pleasant has also been associated with the successful campaign to repeal California’s restriction on Black testimony against white defendants. The law was repealed in 1863, although the precise extent of Pleasant’s personal role is less firmly documented than her later streetcar litigation.4
Between her legal efforts, her financial support for civil rights causes, and her decades of direct assistance to formerly enslaved people building new lives in California, Pleasant became known by a title still used to describe her today: the mother of civil rights in California.4
texts.11:
## Wealth, Scandal, and “Mammy Pleasant”
Historians describe Pleasant as someone who carefully controlled public information about her finances, alliances, and past — a plausible form of self-protection for a wealthy Black woman operating in nineteenth-century San Francisco.2
Pleasant’s later years were shadowed by a business partnership and a controversy that would follow her reputation long after her death. In the 1870s, following her husband’s death, she began investing alongside a wealthy banker, Thomas Bell, and the two built an extensive, closely intertwined financial partnership that included a shared mansion at Bush and Octavia Streets.7
In 1892, the pair purchased a ranch in Sonoma Valley, and their finances remained deeply entangled even after Bell married a much younger woman named Teresa.7 After Bell died from a fall in 1892, his family and Pleasant became locked in lengthy litigation over their deeply intertwined finances. Pleasant ultimately lost control of much of the wealth and property associated with the partnership.7
The legal battles were accompanied by sensational newspaper coverage. Reporters increasingly called her “Mammy Pleasant,” a name Pleasant herself objected to.7
Newspapers also repeated accusations involving fraud, manipulation, and the occult. Those stories became part of the mythology that accumulated around Pleasant and have made it particularly difficult for historians to reconstruct her later life with confidence.2
The Bell/Pleasant residence at Bush and Octavia became central to Pleasant’s later business and legal conflicts. The building no longer stands.10
Pleasant was ultimately declared insolvent before her death in 1904, making the reversal from her earlier financial success all the more striking. Whatever the exact size of her fortune at its height — and estimates vary widely — she had spent decades as a significant investor and property owner in San Francisco.2
According to a later account, Pleasant spent her final months working with a Nevada journalist to record her own version of her life — an attempt to preserve her own account of a life increasingly surrounded by competing stories.7
texts.12:
## Legacy and Civic Relevance
Mary Ellen Pleasant’s life resists a simple summary, and that may be part of why she remains such a compelling figure in California history.
She arrived in Gold Rush San Francisco with capital and multiplied it through investment, property, and business. She used money and influence in support of abolitionist causes and San Francisco’s Black community. She challenged racial exclusion on public transportation through the courts. And by the end of her life, she had become surrounded by enough conflicting stories, lawsuits, newspaper accusations, and self-created mystery that historians are still working to establish where documentation ends and legend begins.2
Her story offers several unusually rich civic questions.
How can an individual use courts to challenge the conduct of powerful institutions? What roles do property, entrepreneurship, philanthropy, churches, newspapers, and civic networks play in building influence outside government? And how should historians evaluate a public figure when autobiographical accounts, court records, newspapers, and later recollections do not always agree?
Pleasant’s life brings all of those questions together. She was simultaneously a businesswoman, investor, abolitionist, litigant, philanthropist, and one of nineteenth-century San Francisco’s most elusive public figures.
Whatever uncertainty remains about Mary Ellen Pleasant’s birthplace, the exact size of her fortune, or some of the stories she told about her own life, the documented record is remarkable enough: she became a successful capitalist in Gold Rush San Francisco, supported abolitionist and Black civic causes, built an extensive network of businesses and property, and challenged racial exclusion through the courts.
Her life accumulated titles, accusations, fortunes, lawsuits, and legends.
But when Pleasant considered how she wanted to be remembered, she chose something much simpler:
**_A friend of John Brown._**

**John Sutter** (born February 15, 1803, Kandern, Baden [Germany]—died June 18, 1880, Washington, D.C.) was a German-born Swiss pioneer settler and colonizer in California. The discovery of gold on his land in 1848 precipitated the California Gold Rush.
Sutter's MillSutter's Mill on the American River, Coloma, California; engraving, _Illustrated History of Plumas, Lassen & Sierra Counties, with California from 1513 to 1850_, 1882.(more)
Sutter spent much of his early life in Switzerland; he was a Swiss citizen and served in the Swiss army. Fleeing from bankruptcy and financial failures and leaving his wife and children in Switzerland, he reached California in 1839 and persuaded the Mexican governor to grant him lands on the Sacramento River. There, at its junction with the American River, he established the colony of Nueva Helvetia (New Switzerland), later to become Sacramento. He built “Sutter’s Fort” (1841), set up frontier industries, and, in spite of his enormous debts, provided lavish hospitality, and often employment, to traders, trappers, and immigrants who came to his fort. Sutter was much less accommodating to the local Native Americans whose labour he exploited.
James W. Marshall testing a gold nuggetJames W. Marshall and Mrs. Wimmer testing one of the first gold nuggets found at Sutter's Mill by boiling it in lye soap; illustration, _California Gold Book: First Nugget, Its Discovery and Discoverers_, by William Wallace Allen and R.B. Avery, 1893.(more)

# John Sutter
Discovery of gold on his land brought disaster to Sutter. In the process of building a water-powered sawmill, a carpenter named James W. Marshall found flakes of gold in a streambed (January 24, 1848). The two men tried to keep the find a secret, but the news leaked out. Workers deserted the colony. Gold seekers and squatters overran Sutter’s land, stealing and destroying his goods and livestock. When the U.S. courts denied title to his Mexican grants, his ruin was complete. By 1852 he was bankrupt.
Sutter's Mill replica Replica of Sutter's Mill, Marshall Gold Discovery State Historic Park, Coloma, California.(more)
In the early 1850s Sutter moved to Hock Farm, his estate on the Feather River, and in 1864 he was awarded a monthly pension by the California legislature. The following year, however, arsonists destroyed his home, and by 1871 Sutter had settled in Lititz, Pennsylvania. He frequently traveled to Washington, D.C., continuing his attempt to gain redress through the U.S. Congress. Sutter Street, in San Francisco, and Sutter County commemorate his name.
The Sutter story was retold in the 1985 song _Sutter’s Mill_ by American singer and songwriter Dan Fogelberg.

The California Gold Rush was a period of rapid migration to California following the discovery of gold at Sutter's Mill in early 1848. This event triggered an influx of over 300,000 fortune seekers, known as "forty-niners," by 1852.

# California Gold Rush
John Augustus SutterThe discovery of gold on Sutter's land in 1848 started the California Gold Rush. (more)
In 1848 John Sutter was having a water-powered sawmill built along the American River in Coloma, California, approximately 50 miles (80 km) east of present-day Sacramento. On January 24 his carpenter, James W. Marshall, found flakes of gold in a streambed. Sutter and Marshall agreed to become partners and tried to keep their find a secret. News of the discovery, however, soon spread, and they were besieged by thousands of fortune seekers. (With his property overrun and his goods and livestock stolen or destroyed, Sutter was bankrupt by 1852.) From the East, prospectors sailed around Cape Horn or risked disease hiking across the Isthmus of Panama. The hardiest took the 2,000-mile (3,220-km) overland route, on which cholera proved a far greater killer than the Native Americans. By August 1848, 4,000 gold miners were in the area, and within a year about 80,000 “forty-niners” (as the fortune seekers of 1849 were called) had arrived at the California goldfields. By 1853 their numbers had grown to 250,000. Although it was estimated that some $2 billion in gold was extracted, few of the prospectors struck it rich. The work was hard, prices were high, and living conditions were primitive.

# California Gold Rush
In what was a typical pattern, the Gold Rush slackened as the most-workable deposits were exhausted and organized capital and machinery replaced the efforts of individual miner-adventurers with more efficient and businesslike operations. Likewise, the lawless and violent mining camps gave way to permanent settlements with organized government and law enforcement. Those settlements that lacked other viable economic activities soon became ghost towns after the gold was exhausted. The California Gold Rush peaked in 1852, and by the end of the decade, it was over.

The Gold Rush had a profound impact on California, dramatically changing its demographics. Before the discovery of gold, the territory’s population was approximately 160,000, the vast majority of whom were Native Americans. By about 1855, more than 300,000 people had arrived. Most were Americans, though a number of settlers also came from China, Europe, and South America. The massive influx gave rise to numerous cities and towns, with San Francisco gaining particular prominence. The Gold Rush was credited with hastening statehood for California in 1850.

_\_\\_\\\_\\\\_How a shrewd Gold Rush businesswoman built a fortune, backed the abolitionist cause, and took racial exclusion in San Francisco to court — while carefully controlling the story of her own life.\\\\_\\\_\\_\__
By the time Mary Ellen Pleasant died in San Francisco in 1904, she had been called a millionaire, a capitalist, a voodoo queen, a madam, and the mother of California’s civil rights movement — sometimes all in the same newspaper column.1
She was one of the most influential Black women in Gold Rush–era San Francisco. Using inherited capital, business skill, and carefully cultivated networks, Pleasant built wealth through lending, gold-and-silver exchange, real estate, mining stock, boardinghouses, and other ventures. She supported abolitionist and Black civic causes, and later challenged racial exclusion on San Francisco streetcars through the courts.1
She was also one of the hardest historical figures to pin down. Pleasant gave differing accounts of her own beginnings, while newspapers and later biographers added layers of rumor and legend. More than a century after her death, historians are still working to separate the documented woman from the mythology surrounding her.2
Mary Ellen Pleasant, San Francisco pioneer, 1901. Miriam Matthews Photograph Collection, UCLA Library Digital Collections.9

## A Story With Many Beginnings
Even the basic facts of Mary Ellen Pleasant’s early life remain disputed. Pleasant said that she was born free in Philadelphia in 1819, while later accounts — including the semi-fictionalized biography _Mammy Pleasant_ — claimed she had been born enslaved in Georgia. The surviving record does not settle the question; what is clear is that, by the 1820s, she was living in Nantucket, Massachusetts.2
In Nantucket, Pleasant worked as a shop clerk and later described the experience as the beginning of her business education. She recalled learning to manage transactions and customers quickly in the busy store environment.2

## A Story With Many Beginnings
### Nantucket and the Hussey Store
The shop belonged to a family remembered as the Husseys. Pleasant became close with the family’s granddaughter, Phebe Hussey Gardner, and stayed in touch with her Nantucket connections for decades, even after she left the island around 1840 and began working more directly within the abolitionist movement.3

## A Story With Many Beginnings
### Boston, Abolition, and Two Marriages
Pleasant later moved to Boston, where she met James Smith, an abolitionist of some means. When Smith died in the 1840s, he left her capital that helped finance her move west. Pleasant later married John James Pleasant, and accounts place her arrival in San Francisco during the early 1850s, though the precise date remains disputed.2

## A Story With Many Beginnings
### Gold Fever and a New Life in San Francisco
John James Pleasant sailed for San Francisco not long after news of the 1848 gold discovery reached the East Coast, finding work as a ship’s cook. Sources differ on whether Pleasant arrived in 1849 or 1852; most accounts place her in San Francisco during the early Gold Rush boom, when the city’s rapid expansion created opportunities in lodging, domestic service, finance, and real estate.2

## From Housekeeper to Capitalist
_San Francisco’s harbor in 1851, photographed during the Gold Rush boom. Sterling C. McIntyre, Library of Congress.8_
Pleasant arrived with inherited capital and put it to work through lending, investment, and business ventures.1
At the same time, she worked as a housekeeper for some of San Francisco’s prominent merchants.1
Over time, her investments expanded dramatically. She became a major investor in real estate and mining stock, with property that eventually extended across the bay to Oakland, and built a financial position unusual for any woman in mid-nineteenth-century San Francisco. She was notoriously guarded about the exact scope of her fortune, a caution that historians attribute partly to savvy and partly to the very real legal and social risks a Black woman of enormous wealth faced in nineteenth-century California.2

## The “Black City Hall”
Pleasant used her wealth and connections in support of San Francisco’s Black community.1 Black newcomers could turn to her network for employment, housing, and practical assistance, and she became so well known as a community resource that she acquired one of her most memorable nicknames: the “Black City Hall.”7
She also contributed to the Athenaeum Building, a library and gathering place for San Francisco’s Black residents, and supported the Black press and the African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church.1

## Financing Freedom: Pleasant and John Brown
Near the end of her life, Pleasant told a reporter that she had helped finance John Brown’s 1859 raid on the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry.1
Pleasant said she had traveled to Canada, met with Brown, and supplied money for his plans. She also claimed authorship of a note associated with Brown and said that her initials had been misread, helping conceal her identity after the raid failed.7
In Pleasant’s telling, she then abandoned her original return ticket and traveled back toward California under less conspicuous circumstances.7
The account became one of the most famous episodes in Pleasant’s biography. But it comes principally from recollections she gave late in life, and documentary support for all of its details is limited. What is much more firmly established is Pleasant’s longstanding involvement in abolitionist circles and her admiration for Brown.2
By her own account, she kept this claimed role a closely held secret for the rest of her life, sharing it only in her final years. She requested that her tombstone identify her simply as “a friend of John Brown” — an inscription not actually added to her grave marker until 1965, more than sixty years after her death.1

## Mother of California’s Civil Rights Movement
Pleasant’s activism did not end with the Civil War. San Francisco’s horse-drawn streetcars in the 1860s frequently excluded Black passengers, and Pleasant became one of the people who challenged that practice.4

## Mother of California’s Civil Rights Movement
### The Streetcar Cases
In 1866, she brought a complaint after being denied service by one streetcar company. Contemporary accounts indicate that she withdrew that complaint after company officials agreed that Black passengers would be permitted to ride.7
Her second case produced a longer legal fight.
Pleasant attempted to board a car operated by the North Beach and Mission Railroad Company while her friend Elizabeth “Lisette” Woodworth was already aboard. Evidence introduced in the resulting case attributed a blunt response to the conductor:
_“We don’t take colored people in the cars.”_ 5
Pleasant sued.
A jury initially awarded Pleasant $500 in damages. The railroad appealed, and in 1868 the California Supreme Court reversed that award, finding insufficient proof of a willful injury by the company.5
The litigation nonetheless mattered. Pleasant’s case became part of a broader series of legal and civic challenges to racial exclusion on San Francisco transit. Later institutional summaries describe the case as helping to end segregated public transportation in the city, but that broader characterization should be distinguished from the appellate court’s narrower reversal of her damages judgment.6

## Mother of California’s Civil Rights Movement
### A Change in the Law
Pleasant has also been associated with the successful campaign to repeal California’s restriction on Black testimony against white defendants. The law was repealed in 1863, although the precise extent of Pleasant’s personal role is less firmly documented than her later streetcar litigation.4
Between her legal efforts, her financial support for civil rights causes, and her decades of direct assistance to formerly enslaved people building new lives in California, Pleasant became known by a title still used to describe her today: the mother of civil rights in California.4

## Wealth, Scandal, and “Mammy Pleasant”
Historians describe Pleasant as someone who carefully controlled public information about her finances, alliances, and past — a plausible form of self-protection for a wealthy Black woman operating in nineteenth-century San Francisco.2
Pleasant’s later years were shadowed by a business partnership and a controversy that would follow her reputation long after her death. In the 1870s, following her husband’s death, she began investing alongside a wealthy banker, Thomas Bell, and the two built an extensive, closely intertwined financial partnership that included a shared mansion at Bush and Octavia Streets.7
In 1892, the pair purchased a ranch in Sonoma Valley, and their finances remained deeply entangled even after Bell married a much younger woman named Teresa.7 After Bell died from a fall in 1892, his family and Pleasant became locked in lengthy litigation over their deeply intertwined finances. Pleasant ultimately lost control of much of the wealth and property associated with the partnership.7
The legal battles were accompanied by sensational newspaper coverage. Reporters increasingly called her “Mammy Pleasant,” a name Pleasant herself objected to.7
Newspapers also repeated accusations involving fraud, manipulation, and the occult. Those stories became part of the mythology that accumulated around Pleasant and have made it particularly difficult for historians to reconstruct her later life with confidence.2
The Bell/Pleasant residence at Bush and Octavia became central to Pleasant’s later business and legal conflicts. The building no longer stands.10
Pleasant was ultimately declared insolvent before her death in 1904, making the reversal from her earlier financial success all the more striking. Whatever the exact size of her fortune at its height — and estimates vary widely — she had spent decades as a significant investor and property owner in San Francisco.2
According to a later account, Pleasant spent her final months working with a Nevada journalist to record her own version of her life — an attempt to preserve her own account of a life increasingly surrounded by competing stories.7

## Legacy and Civic Relevance
Mary Ellen Pleasant’s life resists a simple summary, and that may be part of why she remains such a compelling figure in California history.
She arrived in Gold Rush San Francisco with capital and multiplied it through investment, property, and business. She used money and influence in support of abolitionist causes and San Francisco’s Black community. She challenged racial exclusion on public transportation through the courts. And by the end of her life, she had become surrounded by enough conflicting stories, lawsuits, newspaper accusations, and self-created mystery that historians are still working to establish where documentation ends and legend begins.2
Her story offers several unusually rich civic questions.
How can an individual use courts to challenge the conduct of powerful institutions? What roles do property, entrepreneurship, philanthropy, churches, newspapers, and civic networks play in building influence outside government? And how should historians evaluate a public figure when autobiographical accounts, court records, newspapers, and later recollections do not always agree?
Pleasant’s life brings all of those questions together. She was simultaneously a businesswoman, investor, abolitionist, litigant, philanthropist, and one of nineteenth-century San Francisco’s most elusive public figures.
Whatever uncertainty remains about Mary Ellen Pleasant’s birthplace, the exact size of her fortune, or some of the stories she told about her own life, the documented record is remarkable enough: she became a successful capitalist in Gold Rush San Francisco, supported abolitionist and Black civic causes, built an extensive network of businesses and property, and challenged racial exclusion through the courts.
Her life accumulated titles, accusations, fortunes, lawsuits, and legends.
But when Pleasant considered how she wanted to be remembered, she chose something much simpler:
**_A friend of John Brown._**

**John Sutter** (born February 15, 1803, Kandern, Baden [Germany]—died June 18, 1880, Washington, D.C.) was a German-born Swiss pioneer settler and colonizer in California. The discovery of gold on his land in 1848 precipitated the California Gold Rush.
Sutter's MillSutter's Mill on the American River, Coloma, California; engraving, _Illustrated History of Plumas, Lassen & Sierra Counties, with California from 1513 to 1850_, 1882.(more)
Sutter spent much of his early life in Switzerland; he was a Swiss citizen and served in the Swiss army. Fleeing from bankruptcy and financial failures and leaving his wife and children in Switzerland, he reached California in 1839 and persuaded the Mexican governor to grant him lands on the Sacramento River. There, at its junction with the American River, he established the colony of Nueva Helvetia (New Switzerland), later to become Sacramento. He built “Sutter’s Fort” (1841), set up frontier industries, and, in spite of his enormous debts, provided lavish hospitality, and often employment, to traders, trappers, and immigrants who came to his fort. Sutter was much less accommodating to the local Native Americans whose labour he exploited.

# John Sutter
Discovery of gold on his land brought disaster to Sutter. In the process of building a water-powered sawmill, a carpenter named James W. Marshall found flakes of gold in a streambed (January 24, 1848). The two men tried to keep the find a secret, but the news leaked out. Workers deserted the colony. Gold seekers and squatters overran Sutter’s land, stealing and destroying his goods and livestock. When the U.S. courts denied title to his Mexican grants, his ruin was complete. By 1852 he was bankrupt.
Sutter's Mill replica Replica of Sutter's Mill, Marshall Gold Discovery State Historic Park, Coloma, California.(more)
In the early 1850s Sutter moved to Hock Farm, his estate on the Feather River, and in 1864 he was awarded a monthly pension by the California legislature. The following year, however, arsonists destroyed his home, and by 1871 Sutter had settled in Lititz, Pennsylvania. He frequently traveled to Washington, D.C., continuing his attempt to gain redress through the U.S. Congress. Sutter Street, in San Francisco, and Sutter County commemorate his name.
The Sutter story was retold in the 1985 song _Sutter’s Mill_ by American singer and songwriter Dan Fogelberg.

John Augustus SutterThe discovery of gold on Sutter's land in 1848 started the California Gold Rush. (more)
In 1848 John Sutter was having a water-powered sawmill built along the American River in Coloma, California, approximately 50 miles (80 km) east of present-day Sacramento. On January 24 his carpenter, James W. Marshall, found flakes of gold in a streambed. Sutter and Marshall agreed to become partners and tried to keep their find a secret. News of the discovery, however, soon spread, and they were besieged by thousands of fortune seekers. (With his property overrun and his goods and livestock stolen or destroyed, Sutter was bankrupt by 1852.) From the East, prospectors sailed around Cape Horn or risked disease hiking across the Isthmus of Panama. The hardiest took the 2,000-mile (3,220-km) overland route, on which cholera proved a far greater killer than the Native Americans. By August 1848, 4,000 gold miners were in the area, and within a year about 80,000 “forty-niners” (as the fortune seekers of 1849 were called) had arrived at the California goldfields. By 1853 their numbers had grown to 250,000. Although it was estimated that some $2 billion in gold was extracted, few of the prospectors struck it rich. The work was hard, prices were high, and living conditions were primitive.

# California Gold Rush
In what was a typical pattern, the Gold Rush slackened as the most-workable deposits were exhausted and organized capital and machinery replaced the efforts of individual miner-adventurers with more efficient and businesslike operations. Likewise, the lawless and violent mining camps gave way to permanent settlements with organized government and law enforcement. Those settlements that lacked other viable economic activities soon became ghost towns after the gold was exhausted. The California Gold Rush peaked in 1852, and by the end of the decade, it was over.

It operates bus services, as well as light rail services on the Blue, Green, and Gold lines. SacRT and Yolobus both provide bus services connecting Sacramento with Sacramento International Airport.
Amtrak and its Amtrak California subsidiary operate passenger rail service from the Sacramento Valley station. This station is served by the _Coast Starlight_, the _California Zephyr_, the _Capitol Corridor_, and the _Gold Runner_, which link the region with destinations across California and the United States.
Sacramento International Airport is a major, full-service airport with passenger flights. It is owned by the County of Sacramento. The county also owns Sacramento Mather Airport in Rancho Cordova and Sacramento Executive Airport, both of which are general aviation airports. Sacramento McClellan Airport, formerly McClellan Air Force Base, is a privately owned airport between North Highlands and Rio Linda. There are also privately owned public use airports located in Elk Grove and Rio Linda.
The Sacramento County Department of Transportation (SACDOT)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_County,_California#cite_note-48) maintains approximately 2200 miles of roadway within the unincorporated area. *   39.06-120.732Placer County - Sacramento County's northeastern neighbor stretches from the suburbs of Sacramento to Lake Tahoe and the Nevada border. Named after the Spanish word meaning "sand or gravel deposits containing gold", the county was a hotbed of activity during the Gold Rush. *   38.78-120.533El Dorado County - The name of Sacramento County's northeastern neighbor translates from Spanish as "the gilded/golden", an appropriate title for the county where the California Gold Rush was kicked off after a discovery at Sutter's Mill (near Coloma) in 1848. *   38.44-120.664Amador County - Sacramento County's neighbor to the east, Amador County was home to several mines during the Gold Rush, including the Kennedy Mine in Jackson which was the deepest gold mine of its time. Stockton is the county's largest city and is notable for being the world's most inland natural seaport.  
*   37.93-121.956Contra Costa County - Sacramento County's southwestern neighbor is a primarily residential county that offers a vast array of food, shopping, and lodging options for Bay Area visitors. Interstate 80 is the main east-west route, starting in San Francisco and continuing through the Lake Tahoe region and onwards to Reno. During winter it is one of the few east-west routes through the Sierra Nevada mountains that remains open.

*   39.04-121.691Sutter County - Sacramento County's northwestern neighbor, tiny Sutter County lies between the Sacramento and Feather rivers, with nearly 90% of the county's land used for grazing and agriculture. The county is home to the eroded volcanic lava domes of the Sutter Buttes, which occupy a circular area roughly 10 miles (16 km) across and are sometimes referred to as the world's smallest mountain range.  
*   39.06-120.732Placer County - Sacramento County's northeastern neighbor stretches from the suburbs of Sacramento to Lake Tahoe and the Nevada border. Named after the Spanish word meaning "sand or gravel deposits containing gold", the county was a hotbed of activity during the Gold Rush. Today visitors can enjoy mountain activities such as hiking and skiing, and will also be impressed by the historic courthouse in Auburn.  
*   38.78-120.533El Dorado County - The name of Sacramento County's northeastern neighbor translates from Spanish as "the gilded/golden", an appropriate title for the county where the California Gold Rush was kicked off after a discovery at Sutter's Mill (near Coloma) in 1848. The county's attractions include mountain scenery, gold mining history, the impossibly blue waters of Lake Tahoe, backpacking opportunities in the Desolation Wilderness, and epic skiing in the South Lake Tahoe area.  
*   38.44-120.664Amador County - Sacramento County's neighbor to the east, Amador County was home to several mines during the Gold Rush, including the Kennedy Mine in Jackson which was the deepest gold mine of its time. Today the county is known for its Zinfandel, with the Shenandoah Valley home to over forty wineries. Visitors may also enjoy Black Chasm Cavern in Volcano, historic buildings, and outdoor activities such as skiing, camping and fishing.

*   37.93-121.275San Joaquin County - San Joaquin County lies south of Sacramento County on the eastern edge of the California Delta, an estuary formed by the confluence of the San Joaquin and Sacramento rivers. Nicknamed "California's Holland" due to the extensive levee system, the area is an interesting place to explore by car or boat. Stockton is the county's largest city and is notable for being the world's most inland natural seaport.  
*   37.93-121.956Contra Costa County - Sacramento County's southwestern neighbor is a primarily residential county that offers a vast array of food, shopping, and lodging options for Bay Area visitors. The landscape is dominated by Mount Diablo, a peak that provides excellent hiking opportunities and, on clear days, summit views that stretch for well over 100 miles (160 km) in all directions. Other attractions include the John Muir Historic Site in Martinez, the estate of Nobel winning playwright Eugene O'Neill in Danville, and a WWII shipyard, now a national historic site, in Richmond.  
*   38.27-121.947Solano County - Located southwest of Sacramento County, Solano County is far more rural than the other Bay Area counties, and includes significant portions of the California Delta, as well as parts of San Pablo Bay. Two of the county's cities served as early state capitals: Vallejo was the capital in 1852 and again in 1853, while Benicia served as the capital from February 1853 until February 1854; today Benicia Capitol State Historic Park provides the opportunity for visitors to explore the Capitol building from that era.

Sacramento Regional Transit District, also known as Sacramento RT, provides public transit throughout the county. It operates bus services, as well as light rail services on the Blue, Green, and Gold lines. Amtrak and its Amtrak California subsidiary operate passenger rail service from the Sacramento Valley station. Sacramento International Airport is a major, full-service airport with passenger flights. It is owned by the County of Sacramento. Sacramento McClellan Airport, formerly McClellan Air Force Base, is a privately owned airport between North Highlands and Rio Linda. ## Regional composition
Sacramento is the most populous city in the metropolitan area, home to approximately 526,000 people, making it the sixth-most populous city in California and the 35th most populous in the United States. It has been the state capital of California since 1851 and has played an important role in the history of California. When gold was discovered in nearby [Sutter's Mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutter's_Mill "Sutter's Mill") in Coloma, Sacramento became a boom town luring in migrants making their way from San Francisco to the gold fields of the Sierras. Although it did not become the financial and cultural center of Northern California, titles that were given to San Francisco, Sacramento became the largest transportation hub of not only Northern California, but also the West Coast following the completion of the First Transcontinental Railroad. Sacramento today continues to be one of the largest rail hubs in North America, and its rail station is one of the busiest in the United States. In 2002, Time Magazine featured an article recognizing Sacramento as the most diverse and integrated city in America.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_metropolitan_area#cite_note-7) Government (state and federal) jobs are still the largest sector of employment in the city and the city council does considerable effort to keep state agencies from moving outside the city limits.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_metropolitan_area#cite_note-8) The remainder of Sacramento County is suburban in general with most of the working population commuting to Downtown Sacramento and with a smaller proportion commuting all the way to the Bay Area.
Palisades Tahoe, the site of the 1960 Winter Olympics
Yolo County is a mixture of an agricultural area and commuter region, with most of its working population commuting either to the Bay Area or Sacramento for work. It is home to the University of California, Davis, campus, the northernmost UC campus and only UC campus in the Greater Sacramento region.

## Regional composition
El Dorado and Placer Counties form the remainder of the inner core of Greater Sacramento and are composed of the Sierra Nevada foothills and mountains. The western areas of the counties are composed of commuter suburbs, with Roseville in Placer County being Sacramento's most populous edge city. The Sierra foothills mostly contain residential acreage properties and small farms. The easternmost areas border Lake Tahoe and are home to numerous ski resorts and towns such as South Lake Tahoe, site of the Heavenly Mountain Resort, which are popular in winter months and nature camps and resorts in summer months. Placer County has been an important mining area not only for gold, but also other minerals and granite. It is also the site of Squaw Valley, which hosted the 1960 Winter Olympics, which has been up to date, the only Winter Olympic Games to be held in California and the US West Coast and the smallest city to host an Olympics.
Stateline is an important Tahoe resort town on the shores of Lake Tahoe.
The Yuba–Sutter area consists of Yuba and Sutter counties and is a primarily agricultural area, although the southern area is more suburban in character. It is home to Sunsweet Growers, which owns the world's largest dried fruit plant in Yuba City. Nevada County, like El Dorado and Placer Counties, borders Lake Tahoe and contains numerous ski resorts such as the Boreal Mountain Resort, but is more rural than the former two counties and is an important gold mining area. The Donner Memorial State Park is located in the county, where the ill-fated Donner Party was trapped in winter storms in 1846–47 while attempting to make it to California on a poorly organized trip.
Douglas County, Nevada was recently briefly added to the Sacramento Combined Statistical Area. As Greater Sacramento continues to grow beyond its inner region, Western Nevada continues to be influenced by Sacramento and California and their cultures.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_metropolitan_area#cite_note-9) However, Douglas County has since been removed again from the Sacramento CSA, and transferred to the Reno-Carson City-Fernley, NV CSA.

## Geography and climate
[edit]
A cove inside the Sacramento River delta
The western half of Greater Sacramento is centered on the Central Valley, one of the most vital agricultural areas in the country. The Sierra Nevada and its foothills compose the eastern portion of the region. Yolo County contains a large flood control basin. The Sacramento River and the American River are major rivers that form a deepwater port connected to the San Francisco Bay by a channel through the Sacramento River Delta. Coniferous and oak-dominated woodland are prevalent in the Sierra Nevada and the Lake Tahoe area.
Sacramento and the valley area have a Mediterranean climate (Köppen_Csa_), characterized by damp to wet, cool winters and hot, dry summers. The wet season is generally October through April. Summer heat is often moderated by a sea breeze known as the "delta breeze" which comes through the Sacramento–San Joaquin River Delta from the San Francisco Bay.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_metropolitan_area#cite_note-10) January is the coolest month for the entire region with an average maximum of 41.0°F (5.0°C) and an average minimum of 15.1°F (-9.4°C) in Lake Tahoe.
The eastern portion of Greater Sacramento experiences a more varied climate with 90°F (32.2°C) temperatures in August to below freezing temperatures in winter. In higher elevations, freezing temperatures have been recorded every month. In the winter, below freezing temperatures are common in Sacramento and lower valley elevations although snowfall is scarce and usually melts on ground contact with significant snowfall occurring roughly every 3–5 years. However, blizzard conditions in winter storms can be common in the higher elevations.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_metropolitan_area#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_metropolitan_area#cite_note-12)

## Regional composition
Sacramento is the most populous city in the metropolitan area, home to approximately 526,000 people, making it the sixth-most populous city in California and the 35th most populous in the United States. It has been the state capital of California since 1851 and has played an important role in the history of California. When gold was discovered in nearby [Sutter's Mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutter's_Mill "Sutter's Mill") in Coloma, Sacramento became a boom town luring in migrants making their way from San Francisco to the gold fields of the Sierras. Although it did not become the financial and cultural center of Northern California, titles that were given to San Francisco, Sacramento became the largest transportation hub of not only Northern California, but also the West Coast following the completion of the First Transcontinental Railroad. Sacramento today continues to be one of the largest rail hubs in North America, and its rail station is one of the busiest in the United States. In 2002, Time Magazine featured an article recognizing Sacramento as the most diverse and integrated city in America.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_metropolitan_area#cite_note-7) Government (state and federal) jobs are still the largest sector of employment in the city and the city council does considerable effort to keep state agencies from moving outside the city limits.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_metropolitan_area#cite_note-8) The remainder of Sacramento County is suburban in general with most of the working population commuting to Downtown Sacramento and with a smaller proportion commuting all the way to the Bay Area.
Palisades Tahoe, the site of the 1960 Winter Olympics
Yolo County is a mixture of an agricultural area and commuter region, with most of its working population commuting either to the Bay Area or Sacramento for work. It is home to the University of California, Davis, campus, the northernmost UC campus and only UC campus in the Greater Sacramento region.
texts.4:
## Regional composition
El Dorado and Placer Counties form the remainder of the inner core of Greater Sacramento and are composed of the Sierra Nevada foothills and mountains. The western areas of the counties are composed of commuter suburbs, with Roseville in Placer County being Sacramento's most populous edge city. The Sierra foothills mostly contain residential acreage properties and small farms. The easternmost areas border Lake Tahoe and are home to numerous ski resorts and towns such as South Lake Tahoe, site of the Heavenly Mountain Resort, which are popular in winter months and nature camps and resorts in summer months. Placer County has been an important mining area not only for gold, but also other minerals and granite. It is also the site of Squaw Valley, which hosted the 1960 Winter Olympics, which has been up to date, the only Winter Olympic Games to be held in California and the US West Coast and the smallest city to host an Olympics.
Stateline is an important Tahoe resort town on the shores of Lake Tahoe.
The Yuba–Sutter area consists of Yuba and Sutter counties and is a primarily agricultural area, although the southern area is more suburban in character. It is home to Sunsweet Growers, which owns the world's largest dried fruit plant in Yuba City. Nevada County, like El Dorado and Placer Counties, borders Lake Tahoe and contains numerous ski resorts such as the Boreal Mountain Resort, but is more rural than the former two counties and is an important gold mining area. The Donner Memorial State Park is located in the county, where the ill-fated Donner Party was trapped in winter storms in 1846–47 while attempting to make it to California on a poorly organized trip.
Douglas County, Nevada was recently briefly added to the Sacramento Combined Statistical Area. As Greater Sacramento continues to grow beyond its inner region, Western Nevada continues to be influenced by Sacramento and California and their cultures.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_metropolitan_area#cite_note-9) However, Douglas County has since been removed again from the Sacramento CSA, and transferred to the Reno-Carson City-Fernley, NV CSA.

## Geography and climate
[edit]
A cove inside the Sacramento River delta
The western half of Greater Sacramento is centered on the Central Valley, one of the most vital agricultural areas in the country. The Sierra Nevada and its foothills compose the eastern portion of the region. Yolo County contains a large flood control basin. The Sacramento River and the American River are major rivers that form a deepwater port connected to the San Francisco Bay by a channel through the Sacramento River Delta. Coniferous and oak-dominated woodland are prevalent in the Sierra Nevada and the Lake Tahoe area.
Sacramento and the valley area have a Mediterranean climate (Köppen_Csa_), characterized by damp to wet, cool winters and hot, dry summers. The wet season is generally October through April. Summer heat is often moderated by a sea breeze known as the "delta breeze" which comes through the Sacramento–San Joaquin River Delta from the San Francisco Bay.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_metropolitan_area#cite_note-10) January is the coolest month for the entire region with an average maximum of 41.0°F (5.0°C) and an average minimum of 15.1°F (-9.4°C) in Lake Tahoe.
The eastern portion of Greater Sacramento experiences a more varied climate with 90°F (32.2°C) temperatures in August to below freezing temperatures in winter. In higher elevations, freezing temperatures have been recorded every month. In the winter, below freezing temperatures are common in Sacramento and lower valley elevations although snowfall is scarce and usually melts on ground contact with significant snowfall occurring roughly every 3–5 years. However, blizzard conditions in winter storms can be common in the higher elevations.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_metropolitan_area#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_metropolitan_area#cite_note-12)

## Regional composition
Sacramento is the most populous city in the metropolitan area, home to approximately 526,000 people, making it the sixth-most populous city in California and the 35th most populous in the United States. It has been the state capital of California since 1851 and has played an important role in the history of California. When gold was discovered in nearby [Sutter's Mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutter's_Mill "Sutter's Mill") in Coloma, Sacramento became a boom town luring in migrants making their way from San Francisco to the gold fields of the Sierras. Although it did not become the financial and cultural center of Northern California, titles that were given to San Francisco, Sacramento became the largest transportation hub of not only Northern California, but also the West Coast following the completion of the First Transcontinental Railroad. Sacramento today continues to be one of the largest rail hubs in North America, and its rail station is one of the busiest in the United States. In 2002, Time Magazine featured an article recognizing Sacramento as the most diverse and integrated city in America.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_metropolitan_area#cite_note-7) Government (state and federal) jobs are still the largest sector of employment in the city and the city council does considerable effort to keep state agencies from moving outside the city limits.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_metropolitan_area#cite_note-8) The remainder of Sacramento County is suburban in general with most of the working population commuting to Downtown Sacramento and with a smaller proportion commuting all the way to the Bay Area.
Palisades Tahoe, the site of the 1960 Winter Olympics
Yolo County is a mixture of an agricultural area and commuter region, with most of its working population commuting either to the Bay Area or Sacramento for work. It is home to the University of California, Davis, campus, the northernmost UC campus and only UC campus in the Greater Sacramento region.

## Regional composition
El Dorado and Placer Counties form the remainder of the inner core of Greater Sacramento and are composed of the Sierra Nevada foothills and mountains. The western areas of the counties are composed of commuter suburbs, with Roseville in Placer County being Sacramento's most populous edge city. The Sierra foothills mostly contain residential acreage properties and small farms. The easternmost areas border Lake Tahoe and are home to numerous ski resorts and towns such as South Lake Tahoe, site of the Heavenly Mountain Resort, which are popular in winter months and nature camps and resorts in summer months. Placer County has been an important mining area not only for gold, but also other minerals and granite. It is also the site of Squaw Valley, which hosted the 1960 Winter Olympics, which has been up to date, the only Winter Olympic Games to be held in California and the US West Coast and the smallest city to host an Olympics.
Stateline is an important Tahoe resort town on the shores of Lake Tahoe.
The Yuba–Sutter area consists of Yuba and Sutter counties and is a primarily agricultural area, although the southern area is more suburban in character. It is home to Sunsweet Growers, which owns the world's largest dried fruit plant in Yuba City. Nevada County, like El Dorado and Placer Counties, borders Lake Tahoe and contains numerous ski resorts such as the Boreal Mountain Resort, but is more rural than the former two counties and is an important gold mining area. The Donner Memorial State Park is located in the county, where the ill-fated Donner Party was trapped in winter storms in 1846–47 while attempting to make it to California on a poorly organized trip.
Douglas County, Nevada was recently briefly added to the Sacramento Combined Statistical Area. As Greater Sacramento continues to grow beyond its inner region, Western Nevada continues to be influenced by Sacramento and California and their cultures.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_metropolitan_area#cite_note-9) However, Douglas County has since been removed again from the Sacramento CSA, and transferred to the Reno-Carson City-Fernley, NV CSA.

## Geography and climate
[edit]
A cove inside the Sacramento River delta
The western half of Greater Sacramento is centered on the Central Valley, one of the most vital agricultural areas in the country. The Sierra Nevada and its foothills compose the eastern portion of the region. Yolo County contains a large flood control basin. The Sacramento River and the American River are major rivers that form a deepwater port connected to the San Francisco Bay by a channel through the Sacramento River Delta. Coniferous and oak-dominated woodland are prevalent in the Sierra Nevada and the Lake Tahoe area.
Sacramento and the valley area have a Mediterranean climate (Köppen_Csa_), characterized by damp to wet, cool winters and hot, dry summers. The wet season is generally October through April. Summer heat is often moderated by a sea breeze known as the "delta breeze" which comes through the Sacramento–San Joaquin River Delta from the San Francisco Bay.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_metropolitan_area#cite_note-10) January is the coolest month for the entire region with an average maximum of 41.0°F (5.0°C) and an average minimum of 15.1°F (-9.4°C) in Lake Tahoe.
The eastern portion of Greater Sacramento experiences a more varied climate with 90°F (32.2°C) temperatures in August to below freezing temperatures in winter. In higher elevations, freezing temperatures have been recorded every month. In the winter, below freezing temperatures are common in Sacramento and lower valley elevations although snowfall is scarce and usually melts on ground contact with significant snowfall occurring roughly every 3–5 years. However, blizzard conditions in winter storms can be common in the higher elevations.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_metropolitan_area#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_metropolitan_area#cite_note-12)
